set.st: A mail plane carrying 133 black (industrial) diamonds crashed nose-first and burned in March 1929 in a wheat field on the Ted Knoll farm, eight miles southwest of Harmon; the pilot had parachuted onto a farm about half a mile west. By 1 May 1929 all but 30 stones had been recovered by sifting and the wreck was sold for junk; by 4 June the Rockford paper counted $25,000 worth recovered from tons of sifted mud and 29 stones, worth about $5,000, still missing. No later reports of stones turning up. The Gazette named the pilot as Paul J. Kanuit, flying a Curtiss Falcon. Its reporter reached the wreck from Harmon by going back to the Van Petten road, a mile west, then south 80 rods and about a mile on foot through wheat and corn fields; the nearest station was Van Petten, two and a half miles away. The plane nosed in, leaving a crater with the steel propeller ten feet down, exploded and burned about thirty feet from the hole, and the mail went 'to the four winds'. Pin is approximate, not the spot itself.
set.v: 29 black (industrial) diamonds worth about $5,000 in 1929, still missing after the sifting (133 carried; $25,000 worth recovered)
set.tovw: Lead grade B: four 1929 local papers; 29 of 133 stones never recovered; the field is placed only to the farm, and diamonds will not show on a detector
